entities.name: Assembly of Corsica
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Assembly of Corsica (Assemblée de Corse), established in its current form in 2018 as a merger of the Corsican Regional Council and the General Councils of Haute-Corse and Corse-du-Sud, is the single territorial assembly governing the French island of Corsica — an autonomous collectivity within France that has experienced decades of nationalist movement activity, occasional political violence, and ongoing debate about independence, autonomy, and cultural preservation of the Corsican language and identity.

Corsica's distinctive political status reflects its complex history: a Genoese possession for centuries, transferred to France in 1768 (one year before Napoleon Bonaparte was born there), Corsica has always maintained a strong separate identity from the French mainland. The FLNC (National Liberation Front of Corsica) conducted bombings and attacks from 1976 until its 2014 ceasefire, representing the armed wing of Corsican nationalism. French governments have been cautious about expanding Corsican autonomy, fearing precedent for Brittany, Alsace, and other regions.

The 2018 elections gave Corsican nationalist parties (Gilles Simeoni's Femu a Corsica coalition) an absolute majority in the new Assembly — the first time nationalists held outright power. The Assembly has advocated for co-official status for the Corsican language, tax autonomy, and a special constitutional status for Corsica distinct from mainland French departments. The French government under Emmanuel Macron opened negotiations about Corsican autonomy, making the Assembly's relationship with Paris the defining political question of contemporary Corsica.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Assembly of Corsica — the institutional expression of an island's centuries-long separate identity, achieving nationalist electoral majority in 2018, and conducting the most serious autonomy negotiations with France in modern history — represents a significant test of French unitary republicanism's adaptability to regional distinctiveness.
